players.product: retail colocation & interconnection (IBX data centers, Equinix Fabric) and xScale hyperscale data centers

quarterly_data.signal: First public sizing of the build pipeline behind the raised capex plan. EVP of Global Operations Raouf Abdel: Equinix has 'announced 52 some odd projects that are in flight that have been publicly announced across 33 markets across the globe', with 'another 50 that are in planning, development stage, securing either the land or the power or the supply chain' - '100 projects in the portfolio to work with', of which the back 50 get picked by 'which ones are going to get energy'. Planning horizon has extended: 'We're planning today what we're going to deliver in 2028', and '2028 and 2029', with all land banking, power banking and manufacturing pre-buy done for future delivery. Asked about a 3 gigawatt land bank he said 'Maybe a little overstated, but we are in the multi-gigawatt land bank'. He confirmed the analyst's framing that 80% of the CapEx goes into the top 25 markets ('That's correct, yep').
quarterly_data.figure: 52 some odd projects in flight across 33 markets; another 50 that are in planning; 100 projects in the portfolio; 80% of the CapEx into the top 25 markets; delivery planned for 2028 and 2029

quarterly_data.signal: Forward capacity-delivery run-rate. Asked whether Equinix can reach a cadence of '14,000, 15,000 cabinets a quarter' after pulling 7,000 cabinets forward, Abdel said 'we feel confident that we're going to glide into those levels because we have the plans in place, we have the land banks in place, we have reasonable certainty around energy'. He added that pre-sales are 'higher than they've ever been' - capacity is sold before it is completed - which leaves 'less latitude for slippage', and that if demand keeps increasing Equinix will look at further acceleration within its committed capital envelope.
quarterly_data.figure: 14,000, 15,000 cabinets a quarter; 7,000 cabinets pulled forward

quarterly_data.signal: Build-cost economics disclosed for the first time at this level of detail. Abdel gave an 'indicative range' of build cost of '$10,000-$20,000' depending on geography and project type, and said power connection has gone from free to a major line item: 'Costs us tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site now. It used to cost us nothing.' He is seeing cost inflation in heavily built markets - electricians 'are making $150 an hour these days' - while cost 'definitely moderated on the manufacturing side of the equation'. The response is to shift work offsite: more prefabrication to minimise onsite labour.
quarterly_data.figure: build cost indicative range $10,000-$20,000; tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site; electricians making $150 an hour

quarterly_data.signal: The two binding bottlenecks are energy and trades labour, not demand. Abdel: 'Electricians in many locations are very constrained. There's not enough of them' - electricians and plumbers are 'probably being the most acute' trades. Example given: the greater Chicago metro area has '15 gigawatt' of planned data-center expansions on the docket 'with another 15 that's at least marketed to be planned', and 'there is just not enough electricians'. On power he said generation is 'the tertiary issue' - distribution and transmission are the bottlenecks - and that a site requested the old way 'could be 8 years before you get that power'; Equinix therefore now secures the utility conversation and line of sight to power BEFORE taking down land.
quarterly_data.figure: Chicago metro 15 gigawatt of planned expansions plus another 15 marketed; up to 8 years for power under the old approach

quarterly_data.signal: Fleet density and liquid-cooling retrofit detail. Abdel: Equinix has '280 data centers today' before the announced capacity; asked whether 60 megawatts is now the standard block size he answered 'That's our template'; and cooling is now sized one-for-one with power ('If you are delivering 5 megawatts to a pod, well, you have 5 megawatts of cooling'). Existing sites are not drawn down to 100%, so churn events are backfilled at higher density - 10, 15 kW a cab in a 20-year-old site, not 40, 50 kW - and 'We've also retrofit a bunch of our older data centers with liquid cooling', either direct-to-chip or liquid-to-air. All new builds are liquid-cool ready. He cautioned that headline rack numbers are peaks, not averages: 'one of our latest builds is 18 kW average', which supports 50, 60, 70 kW cabinets alongside 4 and 5 kW ones. Modern designs removed raised flooring, so heat can be placed anywhere inside the pod envelope.
quarterly_data.figure: 280 data centers today; 60 megawatts block size confirmed as 'our template'; cooling matched one-for-one with power (5 megawatts of cooling per 5 megawatts); latest build 18 kW average; 40, 50, 70 kW peak cabinets
